libscanR

Vendor-agnostic analysis and visualization of Laser-Induced Breakdown Spectroscopy (LIBS) data in R, with a focus on biomedical tissue research. This is experimental research software. Synthetic examples and heuristic tissue labels do not establish clinical performance.

Features

  • Import: Generic CSV/TSV/TXT, SciAps Z-series, Applied Spectra J200/Aurora, auto-detection.
  • Preprocessing: SNIP/ALS baseline correction, five normalization modes, Savitzky-Golay / Gaussian / moving-average / median smoothing, shot averaging with outlier removal, wavelength cropping, gate delay optimization.
  • Peak analysis: SNR+prominence peak detection; identification against a user-supplied local atomic reference. No NIST compilation is bundled. Missing transition rates and ambiguous candidates remain explicit; wavelength scores are not probabilities.
  • Calibration: Univariate, internal-standard and PLS prediction with retained wavelength and processing contracts. The two-stage Saha-Boltzmann calculation requires explicit atomic data, partition functions, density and instrument response; it estimates relative elemental number fractions under stated assumptions.
  • Chemometrics: PCA, PLS-DA, k-means / hierarchical clustering, SVM / Random-Forest classifiers.
  • Tissue analysis: Exploratory rule-based tissue labels using elemental ratios; discriminating-line analysis with FDR correction.
  • Spatial mapping: Single-element and multi-element 2-D maps from raster-scan datasets.
  • Visualization: Publication-ready ggplot2 plots; custom theme_libs() and wavelength color scale.
  • Shiny app: Six-tab interactive explorer (ls_run_app()).
  • Reproducible examples: ls_example_data() provides synthetic tissue, calibration, and spatial datasets — no instrument data required.

Installation

Use R 4.1 or newer. Install the source from GitHub, or use install_local(".") from a checkout. Atomic-reference data are optional and downloaded separately; the teaching examples below do not need them.

install.packages("remotes", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
remotes::install_github("CTTIR/libscanR", upgrade = "never")

# Explorer and the optional PLS, SVM, forest and density-clustering methods:
install.packages(c("bslib", "plotly", "DT", "shinyWidgets", "pls", "e1071", "ranger", "dbscan"),
                 repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")

The core requires R and the dependencies in DESCRIPTION. Compiling dependencies from source may require the usual R build tools for your platform. Vignettes are available on the documentation site; for local copies install knitr and rmarkdown, then use remotes::install_local(".", build_vignettes = TRUE, upgrade = "never"). The complete-spectrum ZIP download also needs a ZIP utility on PATH or configured with R_ZIPCMD, including on Windows. The other CSV exports do not require it.

A CRAN release and the previously recorded Zenodo identifier were not confirmed during the maintenance audit on 3 November 2026. No new CRAN or archival release is claimed here.

Quick start 

library(libscanR)

# Generate an explicitly fictional teaching spectrum
spec <- ls_simulate_spectrum(
  line_data = ls_demo_peaks(),
  elements = c(Ca = 5000, Na = 1000, Fe = 200),
  seed = 1
)

# Preprocess: baseline, smooth, normalize
spec_proc <- spec |>
  ls_baseline(method = "snip") |>
  ls_smooth(method = "moving_avg", window = 5) |>
  ls_normalize(method = "total")

# Detect and plot peaks without an atomic reference
peaks <- ls_find_peaks(spec_proc)
ls_plot_spectrum(spec_proc, show_peaks = TRUE)

# Export all shots and metadata for a later import
folder <- tempfile("libs-example-")
ls_export_spectra(ls_dataset(list(spec)), folder)
restored <- ls_read_dir(folder)

# Launch the interactive app (requires the optional explorer packages above)
ls_run_app(data = ls_example_data("tissue"))

Optional atomic-reference setup

Basic import, preprocessing, calibration with an explicit numerical line, chemometrics, mapping, the synthetic Saha example and teaching datasets work without an atomic reference. Atomic identification, element overlays and the default ls_simulate_spectrum() require one. There is no automatic download or fallback to fictional atomic values.

  1. Open the NIST ASD Lines Form and review the provider’s terms. Enter the spectra needed for your experiment, for example Ca I; Ca II. Select nm, your wavelength range, CSV output, eV energies, Aki in s^-1, Vacuum (all wavelengths), observed and Ritz wavelengths, g values and bibliographic references. Use All lines. Request at least two spectra so the CSV contains element and sp_num. Save the downloaded CSV and its actual query URL locally. Do not open/save it through a spreadsheet application before conversion.

  2. Use Python 3.9 or newer (standard library only). The example date and query URL below must be replaced with your actual download date and URL. local-data/ is ignored by Git and source-package builds:

    mkdir -p local-data
# Save your download as local-data/nist-download.csv first.
importer="$(Rscript -e 'cat(system.file("scripts", "import_nist.py", package = "libscanR"))')"
python3 "$importer" local-data/nist-download.csv local-data/atomic-lines.csv \
  --retrieved-date YYYY-MM-DD --source-url 'PASTE_THE_ACTUAL_NIST_QUERY_URL'

    The importer preserves all supplied rows, prefers Ritz wavelengths, retains source references and missing values, flags estimated upper energies, and writes a .provenance.json file with input/output SHA-256 hashes. It refuses unsupported units, ambiguous numeric fields, mixed wavelength media and existing output files. It does not download data or infer persistent-line designations. An air-only file keeps its medium and has no invented vacuum counterpart. Keep the original download with its receipt.

  3. Configure the resulting file in R. An explicit path overrides the option, which overrides LIBSCANR_ELEMENT_DB:

    options(libscanR.element_db = normalizePath("local-data/atomic-lines.csv"))
reference <- ls_element_db(elements = "Ca")
# Or use Sys.setenv(LIBSCANR_ELEMENT_DB = "/absolute/path/atomic-lines.csv")
# Or inspect one file without changing the session:
ls_element_db(path = "local-data/atomic-lines.csv", range_nm = NULL)
id <- ls_identify_peaks(peaks, elements = "Ca")

The reader also accepts an RDS data frame with the documented schema; it retains extra provenance fields. The helper does not certify reference accuracy, licensing, LTE assumptions or instrument response. Do not mix air and vacuum measurement axes. Statistical tissue discrimination remains available without a reference, with annotation_status = "reference_unavailable"; invalid configured files raise an error. See the NIST output documentation for units and atomic-data qualifications.

Scientific inputs and migration

The old bundled atomic table is removed. User reference files must explicitly state source and air/vacuum convention; missing rates are not invented. Configure them using the steps above. Existing simulations that relied on the old table must either configure a real reference or explicitly select the fictional teaching input. ls_example_data() always uses fictional peaks with invented strengths; its tissue/component labels are teaching labels, not biological ground truth. Simulated spectra retain the source type and teaching peak table in metadata.

Old calibration and classifier objects that lack an explicit feature contract must be refitted. Tissue output now uses score, score_type and status in place of the ambiguous confidence column; PLS-DA predictions use score instead of a probability label. Keep the training wavelength axis and processing sequence for new samples, including any internal-standard line. Align mismatched axes deliberately; the reader and dataset constructor do not silently relabel channels.

For a complete, fictional two-stage LTE calculation:

source(system.file("examples", "saha-boltzmann-synthetic.R", package = "libscanR"))
result <- do.call(ls_saha_boltzmann, saha_synthetic_example())
result  # X = 0.7, Y = 0.3; temperature = 10000 K
attr(result, "assumptions")

These fractions cover only the supplied elements. The method does not verify LTE, optical thinness, spectral resolution or matrix-independent ablation. Use measured instrument response and independently justified physical inputs for research data. Old results from the incomplete Saha-Boltzmann implementation must be recalculated.

Software: MIT © Raban Heller. No NIST reference compilation, selected source rows or legacy atomic table is distributed in this source tree or package. References downloaded by users retain their providers’ terms; the software license grants no rights in those files. See inst/NOTICE-NIST.md.

Use of LLM tools

Where applicable, LLM tools were used for narrowly defined, non-authorial tasks: copyediting, prose refinement, Markdown/LaTeX formatting, boilerplate scaffolding (such as CI configurations and build scripts), and code refactoring. Tools included Chat AI, the KISSKI (GWDG) service, and self-hosted Mistral Small (24B, Apache-2.0) served through a local vLLM architecture on an Ubuntu Linux workstation with Intel processors and NVIDIA GPUs. The self-hosted model ran locally, with no data sent to third parties.

All scientific claims, methodological choices, analyses, interpretations and conclusions remain the authors’ own. Where applicable, LLM-generated material must be reviewed and revised before inclusion, and references must be verified against their DOI, arXiv ID or ISBN.

Local software setup: vLLM with Python/PyTorch, plus R and RStudio.
